article_raw.title: The Number on the Tip Screen
article_raw.full_story:
<<HOOK>>You reach the payment screen with one tip amount in mind, but the screen shows a higher one.<</HOOK>>

A 2014 research study looked at more than 13 million credit-card taxi payments in New York City. Before payment, the screen showed a few suggested tip rates. The study found that these first numbers had a strong effect on the final tip.

Researchers compared taxi rides with fares just below and just above 15 dollars. The menus changed at this point, so the researchers could make a close comparison. Passengers who saw higher suggested rates left more money. But when the suggested rate was too high, some passengers chose zero instead of changing the amount to a lower tip.

A 2022 policy report from Rutgers University says American restaurant tipping rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent in the late 1990s. Today, some digital screens show tips as high as 35 percent. The report says this can create social pressure, sometimes called “guilt tipping,” because workers may see the customer’s choice.

A 2026 Popmenu survey shows growing frustration. Seventy-eight percent of people said tipping had become ridiculous, and 44 percent said they had lowered their tips from the year before. These are people’s reports, so they do not prove that tip screens caused the change. But the message is clear: the first number can guide a choice, while a number that feels too high can push people away.
article_raw.point_one_body: The taxi study made a close comparison. A ride just below 15 dollars and a ride just above 15 dollars cost almost the same, but the tip menu changed. When the first suggested rate was higher, passengers tipped more. This shows that the number on the screen itself affected credit-card tips in these taxi rides.
article_raw.point_two_body: The pressure is not only about numbers. The Rutgers report says a cash tip jar gave people a more private choice. On a digital screen, a worker may be standing nearby and see the choice. In the Popmenu survey, 59 percent said a digital prompt made them feel they had to tip, down from 66 percent in September 2025.
article_raw.in_one_line: The first tip number can raise payment, but a number that feels too high can make some people choose zero.

article_raw.title: Why Tip Screens Start So High
article_raw.full_story:
<<HOOK>>Imagine standing at a payment screen, with a tip number waiting for you.<</HOOK>>

Why can the first number matter so much? A 2014 study, checked by other experts, looked at more than 13 million credit-card payments in New York City taxis. The screen showed a few suggested tip rates before payment.

Near a $15 fare, the screen changed its suggested choices. Researchers compared rides just below and just above that line. The fares were almost the same, but the screen was different. Passengers who saw the higher suggestions left more tip. But when the suggestion was too high, some chose zero instead of entering a smaller custom amount.

A 2022 report from Rutgers University gives a wider picture. It says US restaurant tipping rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent in the late 1990s. Digital payment screens can show a tip of up to 35 percent. The report says this can create social pressure, because an employee may be in front of the customer and see the choice. It calls this “guilt tipping.”

In a 2026 US consumer survey by Popmenu, 78 percent said tipping had become ridiculous. Forty-four percent said they tipped less than the year before. These are people’s own survey answers, so they do not prove that screens caused the change. But they show strong frustration. The main lesson is simple: the first tip number can lift a payment, but in the taxi study, a very high number also led some card users to choose zero.
article_raw.point_one_body: Near the $15 line, the riders were taking rides with prices just below or just above the same line. The key difference was the first suggested tip menu. This close comparison helps show that the screen affected the tip, rather than the ride price alone.
article_raw.point_two_body: Consumer anger is clear in the survey, but the numbers need care. They are answers from survey participants, not a test of what a screen caused. In the same 2026 survey, 59 percent said a digital screen made them feel they had to tip. That was lower than 66 percent in September 2025.
article_raw.in_one_line: The first tip number can shape the choice, but a very high one can backfire.

final_article_text:
# The First Number on the Tip Screen

You look at a tip screen, and the first numbers you see may change your choice.

A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card taxi payments in New York City. Near a $15 fare, the screen suddenly showed a different set of first tip choices. Passengers who saw higher suggested rates left more money. This shows that the first number can become a starting point for the customer.

But a higher suggestion can also have a bad result. When the suggested tip was too high, some customers did not choose a smaller amount. Instead, they chose no credit card tip at all.

Tip customs have also changed. A Rutgers policy report says restaurant tips in the United States rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent in the late 1990s. Today, digital screens can show tips as high as 35 percent. The report says this can create social pressure, sometimes called “guilt tipping.”

Many customers now feel unhappy about this system. In a 2026 Popmenu survey, 78 percent said tipping had become silly, and 44 percent said they had lowered their tips from the year before. These are people’s reported feelings and actions. They do not prove that tip screens caused the change.

### A Simple Test in New York

The taxi study used rides with fares just below and just above $15. The fares were very close, but the tip choices on the screen changed. This gave the researchers a fair way to compare customers. The result was clear: seeing a higher first choice led to higher tips, although the study did not give one exact increase.

### Pressure in Front of Other People

A cash tip jar can feel private. On a digital screen, the worker may be standing in front of the customer during the choice. The Rutgers report says this can make people feel pressure to tip. In a 2026 survey, 59 percent said a screen made them feel they had to leave a tip.

## In one line…

The first tip number can guide a payment, but if it is too high, some people may choose zero.
